newsitem.title: CANADA: Unity debate becomes new Canadian campaign issue.
newsitem.headline: Unity debate becomes new Canadian campaign issue.

text.p: Politicians campaigning for Canada's June 2 election sparred on Wednesday over whether to hold a new debate on keeping the country together after the moderator of a televised debate collapsed on Tuesday night.
The sole scheduled French-language debate of the campaign abruptly ended when moderator Claire Lamarche fainted, just as the leaders were about to address the Quebec separation issue.
Whether to debate again emerged on Wednesday morning as a new issue, with separatist Bloc Quebecois leader Gilles Duceppe suggesting that Prime Minister Jean Chretien might prefer to hide.

"Perhaps he does not want to answer," Duceppe said, accusing Chretien of ducking his question in an English-language debate on Monday on whether he would abide by Quebeckers' wishes if they voted for sovereignty.
The French-language debate was two hours into its 2-1/2-hour scheduled time when Lamarche fainted. But for Quebeckers, the most interesting part was about to start.

A journalist had just asked Chretien, who came within one percentage point of losing a 1995 referendum on Quebec sovereignty, whether he would abide by a narrow "Yes" vote in favour of splitting from Canada.
The sovereignty issue is especially sensitive for Chretien, leader of the Liberal Party and a French-speaker from Quebec -- where he is, ironically, unpopular.
On Wednesday, his right-wing rivals, the leaders of the Conservative and Reform parties, also called for a new debate.
"As of today we're making it very clear that we're ready to debate this matter," said Conservative leader Jean Charest, who won favourable media coverage for his debate performance.

Reform leader Preston Manning challenged other leaders to come to a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) discussion in English on national unity on Wednesday night and, failing that, to conclude the debate in another forum.
"We would like to have one more debate on this subject," he told a news conference.
No party said it did not want another debate, but some officials said it would be difficult to reschedule one in the less than three weeks of campaigning left.

"We are now negotiating with the other parties to try and get that final half hour rescheduled," Liberal Transport Minister David Anderson told a CBC news conference. But he added: "It's a difficult business for technical reasons."
New Democratic Party (NDP) leader Alexa McDonough said she was willing to join another debate but also mentioned scheduling problems.
Apart from national unity, much of the campaign has centred on how to cut Canada's 9.6 percent unemployment rate, and whether there was still a role for big government.
The NDP and the Bloc Quebecois have argued for more spending, especially for the poor, while Reform and the Conservatives pressed for tax cuts.

In Monday's English-language debate Chretien was hammered by all four parties, particularly over what they said were broken promises made in the 1993 election. But on Tuesday he appeared better able to fight back in his native French.
The abrupt end to the debate, just before the Quebec issue was raised, was a setback for the Bloc Quebecois, founded in 1990 to promote Quebec sovereignty.
